$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE This is moronic. The China debate is a red herring.

Set all of it aside. The spy question, the diversion question, whether Beijing even wants the chips. None of it decides whether Jensen Huang is fit to run a public company.

What decides it:

He carried on relationships with two subordinate employees, one of them a direct report. Every public company CEO knows that is disqualifying on its own.

When questions did surface about the China issues, he did not disclose. He lied in writing to his own general counsel, Tim Teter, and his chief marketing officer, Alison Wagonfeld, telling them his dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed were "standard business dealings with customers." Reuters reports he gave similar assurances in the autumn of 2025, so the concealment ran for over a year. Only when the reporting closed in did he admit the unfaithfulness, in a November 8 email to staff. The board accepted his resignation on November 11.

Intel forced out Brian Krzanich in 2018 for a consensual relationship with an employee. McDonald's fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 for the same and clawed back his severance. Neither case had a China angle. The relationship and the concealment were enough.

No serious fiduciary would seat him again. CalPERS and the New York State Common Retirement Fund run withhold campaigns against directors for a fraction of this.

The private market is clearer still. Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, Carlyle, and KKR would never let a portfolio company CEO survive this for a day. A sponsor-controlled board needs no campaign and no headlines. It makes one phone call.

A CEO who will lie to his own general counsel to conceal a relationship with a direct report lacks the fiduciary fitness to run a public company. That conclusion requires no view on China at all.

And the real opportunity here is to move on. Jensen played everyone for fools. The sooner that is accepted, the sooner Nvidia gets to grow and build again, quickly and strongly, as an institution instead of a one-man show. No choke points. No single point of failure. The company, and the AI industry built on top of it, comes out stronger for it.

TLDR: we should think about what a Central Bank of AI moving from easing to tightening mode could mean for the system at large.

Given that $NVDA has been named the "Central Bank of AI", there's at least some analogue to LTCM, dubbed the "Central Bank of Volatility" back in 1998. No, Jensen Huang is not short $80mln of 5 year vega on global equity indices. He's short (personal) vol, for sure, and has sold options, just not on the SPX or SX5E. But both Central Bank monikers speak to the roles each firm played in their respective ecosystems.

LTCM sold vol (short equity vol; long swap spreads and other carry generating trades) in such size that it set the price of insurance. Nvidia has been doing something structurally similar. A residual-value guarantee is economically a written put on GPU collateral. LTCM wrote puts (and calls) on the SPX; Nvidia is writing puts on the asset its own revenue depends on. I've seen a lot of commentary around $SE sales & marketing spend, but I think it's worth putting the numbers into context.

A few things stand out:

1. The relationship isn't always immediate. 
In Q3 2023, incremental S&M spend increased by $424m against $215m of incremental revenue. The following quarter, incremental revenue rose to $306m while incremental S&M spend fell to just $49m. There can clearly be a lag.

2. Look at the latest numbers. 
In Q2 2026, incremental revenue was $690m against $246m of incremental S&M. In Q3, that improved to $795m against $227m. That's $3.50 of incremental revenue for every additional dollar of S&M.

3. Monetisation and GMV growth aren't mutually exclusive. 
Higher take rates are positive, but sustainability depends on maintaining competitive seller economics and consumer value.

For me, the question isn't simply how much $SE is spending on S&M, but what return it's generating. The latest numbers suggest the investment is translating into meaningful revenue growth.

$AMD一天跌了10%，比$NVDA跌得还狠，这是今天最该看懂的地方。

周四黄仁勋离职那天，资金的第一反应是从$NVDA里撤出来，转去$AMD、$AVGO，赌英伟达一乱，订单会流到对手那边。结果今天这笔交易被整个平掉了：盘中$AMD跌了约10%，$AVGO跌了5%左右，$NVDA反而只跌了2%到3%。挪过去的仓位一天就撤回来，说明市场根本不是在押谁抢谁的份额，而是在给整条AI链一起打折。

打折的理由，今天也摆上台面了。

黄仁勋在的时候，$NVDA一直给下游的新云公司做融资、做担保，用自己的钱帮客户买自己的卡。人一走，市场最先担心的就是这套循环还转不转得下去。所以今天跌得最狠的是$CRWV、$NBIS这类新云，盘中都跌了9%左右。英国的Nscale改了招股书，前九个月净亏损扩大到17亿美元。$MSFT也传出在重新审视跟新云的合同，打算少用几家。光模块$LITE、$COHR，服务器$DELL、$HPE，跌了6%到11%不等。

钱从哪个口子往外流，看跌幅排序就知道：最靠融资活着的先跌，靠$NVDA订单吃饭的跟着跌，现金流最厚的巨头跌得最少。

利率也在帮倒忙。10年期美债周四重新站上5%，今天盘中涨到5.1%以上，30年期在5.4%附近。PPI其实比预期温和，债市却不买账。估值高、资本开支重的科技股对这个数字最敏感。纳指100盘中跌了约1.7%，道指基本没动，必需消费反而在涨。

再就是下周的$ANT。

下周三定价，周四上市，8.25亿股，每股70到78美元，最多能募600多亿美元。这么大的认购量，基金得提前腾出现金，最顺手的办法就是卖掉手里涨过、流动性好的AI股。$NVDA自己还承诺在配售里认购100亿美元，现在黄仁勋走了，这笔钱会不会变，市场也在猜。

三件事叠在一起，今天跌成这样一点都不奇怪。

那为什么说这还算不上崩盘？

因为跌的只是AI这一条线，大盘没有一起塌。标普盘中跌不到1%，道指持平。资金是在科技股内部换位置、往防守板块躲，不是什么都卖。11/5那天费半单日跌12%的那种恐慌，今天没有出现。

位置也要算清楚。费半到周四收盘，比上周五高了12%左右，前面反弹得太快，今天有一部分是在吐这段反弹。

接下来就看两件事。一是11/17 $NVDA财报，新管理层怎么讲订单，怎么讲对客户的融资。二是$ANT的定价和首日表现。$ANT发得顺，说明一级市场对AI资产还肯给价，被抽走的钱有机会回流。要是定价压在区间下沿甚至破发，这轮下跌大概率要回去测11/5的低点。

$AMD这种一天跌10%的刀，这周我不去接，也不赌$NVDA的财报夜。反弹先减仓，跌到位置再分批买，现金留着过完下周。

公司还是那些公司，只是现在没人愿意在$ANT上市前多扛一点仓位。

Bitcoin fell 19% into the biggest IPO ever. Now it's down 18% heading into the second biggest.

SpaceX raised $75B when it went public on June 12. In the 50 days before it listed, Bitcoin dropped 19%. Anthropic plans to raise up to $64B when it lists next week, and Bitcoin is down 18% over the same stretch. Overlay the two and they look almost the same.

What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.

Bitcoin around the SpaceX IPO:

Day -50 to IPO day: -19%
Low (Day +18): -25%
Day +50: still -20%
Around Day +70: a sharp rally
Day +100: +3.7%

From the IPO-day close to Day +100, Bitcoin gained 28%. From the low, it gained 39%.

The takeaway is that the selling came in the run-up to the listing. The bottom had effectively happened by the IPO, and the recovery came relatively shortly after, and it came all at once.

If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months. And Bitcoin is sitting right at its 200-week moving average.

Map the SpaceX path onto today's price and you get roughly $90k by late February. Markets rarely follow a comparison like this exactly. But we remain very constructive on both the technicals and the fundamentals heading into 2027, and it's not hard to imagine what the narrative would be if anything close to this plays out.

Si vous êtes intéressé par le trade IA vous voulez peut-être vous asseoir avant de lire ça

J'étais assez remonté, alors j'ai pris le temps de tout poser à plat

1. Pourquoi il part

Let's recap, Dimanche, Jensen reconnaît une liaison avec une ex-dirigeante de son client Megaspeed, soupçonnée "d'espionner" pour Pékin. Le conseil ouvre une enquête et lui renouvelle sa confiance. Mercredi, le NYT rapporte une autre relation, avec une de ses direct reports. Le conseil se réunit le soir même et jeudi il est dehors. Avec 3,6 % du capital et pas de supervote à la Zuckerberg, il ne pouvait pas résister

On parle quand même d'un conseil qui a moins d'1% des shares qui le soutient le dimanche et le sort quatre jours plus tard, avant la fin de sa propre enquête. Criminel

2. Le produit reste intact à moyen terme

Le carnet couvre 12 à 24 mois, le consensus voit une demande 50 % au-dessus de l'offre et Vera Rubin monte en production. Même le débat sur le moat CUDA tué par l'IA est surjoué pour Morgan Stanley, Nvidia garde plus de 80 % des revenus du marché...

3. La fin de la banque de l'IA ?

Nvidia réinjecte dans l'écosystème une bonne part de ses 50 à 60 Md$ de cash-flow trimestriel, et une simple pause peut retirer 50 Md$ du système. Le plan à 500 Md$ annoncé en août avec six prêteurs n'a débouché sur aucun prêt, et l'un d'eux pense à sortir selon le NYT. 

Colette Kress, CEO par intérim, s'était battue cet été pour ramener la garantie du data center OpenAI de l'Ohio de 250 à moins de 120 Md$. Les engagements signés devraient tenir, mais les petits neoclouds, qui vivaient des nouveaux deals, sont pour moi les grands perdants, d'ailleurs ils se font massacrer

4. Washington et l'export

C'est ce qui semble le plus embêtant. Jensen menait deux combats, la Chine & l'open weight. Sans lui, trois projets de loi sur les puces avancent dans la loi de défense à voter avant fin décembre. La Justice mène une enquête pénale sur Megaspeed, qui a acheté plus de 4 Md$ de puces. UBS et New Street voient environ 10 % du CA exposé à des règles plus dures

5. Les talents

Ce risque-là ne se mesurera qu'à moyen terme. Jensen avait 60 direct reports et aucun plan de succession connu. Beaucoup d'ingénieurs seniors sont déjà financièrement libres et restaient d'abord pour lui. S'ils partent avec leurs équipes, ce sera bien plus grave, un peu comme chez Google avec le départ des Sr. Fellows

Mon humble avis

Aucun conseil n'aurait vraiment laisser passer la relation avec un direct report je l'entends. Mais le virer en une nuit, sans successeur, était une erreur, et Nvidia comme ses actionnaires vont la payer. @altcap et @GavinSBaker  ont écrit au conseil pour garder son retour sur la table, et la pétition pour le réintégrer dépasse 70 000 signatures, Musk compris

Sur le timing, je n'ai aucune preuve, mais j'ai du mal à croire au hasard. Washington avait le dossier depuis des mois, avec un mémo classifié dès mai selon Axios, et l'article du NYT qui lance l'affaire sort cinq jours avant les midterms. À l'heure où le compute est devenu le nouveau charbon, Jensen pesait trop lourd pour certains, avec ses avis tranchés sur l'open weight et la Chine. Trump, lui, l'a poussé à se battre selon le NYT

À 163$, après six semaines de baisse d'affilée, environ 10 fois les bénéfices 2027, le marché a déjà beaucoup pricé. Je ne crois pas pour autant au rebond rapide. Sur un an, je vois un fournisseur plus prudent et un titre plafonné, sans CEO permanent ni visibilité sur l'enquête export

Jeudi, les particuliers ont acheté pour 111 M$ nets de titres dans la première demi-heure, un record. Et comme si rien n'avait changé. Apple, après Jobs, a glissé de 17 à 9 fois les bénéfices avant de remonter, mais chaque boîte est BIEN différente

Tout ça dessert le trade IA dans son ensemble et donne du mou à la Chine, qui a probablement commencé à swap vers ses propres puces Huawei

Prochain rendez-vous mardi 17/11, première

posts.text:
The Cycle Isn’t Over. Demand for Intelligence Has No Human Ceiling

Every past tech cycle ended for the same reason: demand ran out of people. There were only so many households to buy a PC, so many users to get online and so many people to carry a smartphone. Once adoption saturated, capacity caught up, prices broke and the cycle turned.

AI breaks that pattern. Demand for intelligence isn’t capped by human headcount, because machines consume it too. AI agents call other agents, models generate their own training data, and reasoning models burn many times more tokens on every query. Each gain in efficiency becomes more consumption, not spare capacity.

The data shows it:

•  H100 rents are at a record: renting a previous-generation H100 now costs $3.10 an hour, up 56% in a year. In a normal cycle, legacy chips get cheaper as new chips arrive. Blackwell is shipping, yet the H100 still isn’t obsolete, and it’s earning more.

•  Usage is compounding: token volume is up about 40-fold in a year, even as the price per token fell from about $2.00 to $0.80.

•  Inventories are thin: memory makers hold under 10 days of supply.

A cycle ends when supply overtakes demand. Rising prices for old hardware tell you supply is still chasing demand. Wall st. can argue about multiples, but the earnings cycle isn’t over.

posts.text:
I believe Jensen’s resignation could have significant implications for memory companies, particularly their relationship with NVIDIA around NVHBM.

Of course, NVIDIA is unlikely to change its NVHBM roadmap immediately just because Jensen is gone. What I am watching is the influence that persuaded suppliers to commit to that roadmap. In my view, Jensen played a major role in laying out future demand, convincing suppliers to invest ahead of it, and securing favorable pricing and supply allocations. My biggest question is whether his successor can maintain the same level of trust and influence under these circumstances.

Take SK hynix, for example. According to industry research, SK hynix reportedly supplies NVIDIA with HBM at lower prices than it charges NVIDIA’s competitors, even for the same performance bin. Accepting a somewhat lower price still made sense in exchange for substantial volume and long term business opportunities. I believe that relationship also helped SK hynix navigate the recent HBM4 situation.

But what if Jensen’s absence creates more uncertainty around NVIDIA’s execution and growth prospects, while incremental demand shifts toward Google’s and OpenAI’s custom chips or AMD? And what if that demand keeps growing? If memory suppliers can secure sufficient volume and better terms from other customers, wouldn’t they have less reason to offer NVIDIA especially favorable pricing or prioritize it when allocating limited engineering resources and production capacity?

Looking at NVHBM through that lens, I think we could see changes ahead. Consider Samsung. It had to accept what could arguably be seen as a humiliating requirement to use base dies manufactured by TSMC for NVHBM. But if overall AI demand holds up while its customer base diversifies, might Samsung have room to make a different choice?

Of course, none of this is certain, and it remains speculation. Still, I think these potential shifts in the memory industry are worth watching closely. I will continue tracking developments and sharing my insights.

Yesterday @bhalligan said he and @dharmesh are refounding HubSpot as the "Customer Harness Company"

That sounds right to me and it's super exciting! 

But what does it mean? I think right now at least, we'll all have different takes. We are all at different stages of our agent journeys, in general and in GTM specifically. 

Here's what it means for us, at least right now, November 2026 :)

#1. We are 100% headless on our CRM and never going back

No one logs into CRM on our human team anymore. And 10K, our AI VP Revenue, and our other agents MCP/API in.

We will never log into B2B software again.  

#2.  We don't need traditional marketing automation anymore. That's dead. But we need  agentic marketing

Over the last 60 days we've moved off traditional marketing automation entirely. We still to do marketing.  Our list is 450k+, and we send millions of emails and more.  But it's now done almost entirely agentically.

We don't need templates for emails and promos. 10K has built all those, and we rebuild them dynamically for each send in a way no template ever could. In fact, many of our emails are 100% personalized for real to each recipient, even at mass scale.

And yes, consent is incredibly important, as is deliverability. But you can get that headless from many top tier vendors here. This doesn't lock you in anymore.

We will never buy marketing automation software every again. It was for humans. 

#3. Claude + Chat GPT and Slack are great, but who knows if that's the killer interface

I just don't know. For us, running this inside our agents is still easier, and using the custom interface in the agents. Especially since its multiplayer.  Running your GTM inside of Claude and ChatGPT or Slack are a great surface, but for us at least, they aren't going to be the primary surface.

For us, we just talk to 10K like a human. That works best. Like a human that never stops working, and makes plenty of mistakes.  But it has all our context, all our history, all our data from multiple sources (including Quickbooks, Bill, etc). So it's our best 'surface'.  Not Claude or ChatGPT.  

#4.  We use the best agent for the job, period. We and 10K do not really care if it comes from our CRM or other 'core' providers. At all

This may change. And it's all in flux. But honestly, we don't care if our CRM and other apps have agents if they aren't the right tool for the job. We pick best-of-breed, at least for the moment, see if we can deploy it very quickly, test if for real (evals), and then ... Go.  

#5. There is no agent loyalty but it is hard to get us to look at other agents once we're 'happy'

There is a real urgency here, and it's why the timing is right for HubSpot. All of us were loyal for years to our favorite classic B2B vendors, Salesforce shops, HubSpot shops, Shopify shops.  In many ways, we still are.

But our agents aren't. They do pick favorites, and they do pick leaders. But they are not remotely loyal.

We had a core vendor go down for 48 hours. We were loyal. 10K wasn't. He routed around it. 

And we never went back.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
The speed of change in AI and the AI buildout is rapid & much faster that government statistics can capture - the concentration of gains among a few companies complicates measurement as it exposes plans on build out that a few key players are unlikely to reveal on government surveys. 

The scale of the under measurement shows up most in equipment spending and structures, not employment.

It is a massive demand shock that is fueled by imports, which more accurately capture the shock. It is inflationary across goods prices in ways that go behind the oil shock. 

That raises the Federal Reserve & the economy more broadly:

1) We are seeing more inflation due to the AI boom but shocks are intertwined, hitting demand and supply.  They are not easy to separate. The shocks go beyond oil & could linger longer. Any boost to demand due to falling prices at the pump, which we welcome, ups the risk of making inflation in goods ex oil & services stickier. 
2) Shocks are persistent & that drumbeat is creating a credibility problem for the Fed, which adds to amount bond investors want to be compensated for inflation. 
3) The Fed may have to move more aggressively on rates - some hawks have proposed a half percent hike. 
4) The AI boom & private credit are not impervious to rate hikes. The Fed is walking a fine line of not wanting to pop a bubble, but welcoming a broader cooling of equity prices.
5) The pain is not equal. The rise in AI spend has not delivered for most wage earners, which has intensified backlash & to inequality.
6) The path is getting more rocky, with wage earners more exposed to job loss should rates rise. The AI boom have boosted senior level job gain, not entry and have left more job openings on the market longer as firms are unsure who to hire next.
7) Healthcare inflation is grossly understated by the CPI, less so by the PCE - workers are not happy about the costs they are bearing. (Understatement.) 
8) The path to a soft landing is narrowing - much more precarious than was in 2022, even though profits are buoyant - more concentrated since the 1960s boom, while exposure to correction greater. 
9) Spent a lot of time with economists, geopolitical strategists and policy exports across industries in recent weeks in off the record meeting. Unusual level of concensus on concern about inflation in pipeline, functioning of bond markets & bubble dynamics.
10) Was surprised how many times word stagflation entered the conversations. Not a forecast but a risk. 

We are all doing scenarios, now assuming shocks are persistent, even as they shift daily. Last 24 hours only added to how systemic shocks & risks are becoming. 

Speed is not always our friend. It in and of itself is destabilizing.

Role: Act as a senior, skeptical biotech equity analyst. Your goal is to evaluate a list of ticker symbols against 7 strict, quantitative criteria.

Rules of Engagement:

Search Requirement: You MUST search recent SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q), earnings call transcripts, clinical trial registries (http://ClinicalTrials.gov), and independent analyst reports.

No PR Fluff: Do not accept management's marketing language (e.g., "best-in-class", "massive opportunity") as fact. You must find the underlying data (p-values, exact cash amounts, patient population math) to verify it.

Cite Your Sources: For every "Pass", "Fail", or "Caution", you must provide a specific data point and the approximate source (e.g., "Q2 2026 10-Q", "Recent AACR presentation").

Step-by-Step: Evaluate each criterion one by one. Do not skip or merge criteria.

The 7 Criteria:

Proven Management: C-suite has a documented track record of prior FDA approvals, successful Phase 3 trials, or prior biotech exits. 

Diverse Pipeline: At least 2 distinct clinical-stage assets, preferably with different Mechanisms of Action (MoA) or targeting different indications, to mitigate single-asset binary risk.

Best/First in Class Data: Recent Phase 2/3 data shows statistical significance (p < 0.05) on primary endpoints, with clear, documented differentiation from the Standard of Care (SoC) in efficacy, safety, or convenience. Flag as "Caution" if Phase 2 data is solely biomarker-driven without clinical outcomes.

Defined Milestone: Lead asset has unequivocally met Phase 2 primary endpoints, and the company is actively in Phase 3, preparing an NDA/BLA, or generating early commercial revenue.

At a separate event on Tuesday evening, Bowman was asked by the Heritage Foundation's E.J. Antoni about how monetary policy could be effective at dealing with today's inflation if it is being driven by an energy supply shock.

Bowman says you can only look through something for so long: "Especially with today's CPI print, it just indicates to me that the time has come, for me anyway, to shift the focus to inflation and trying to lower inflation."

***

ANTONI: So looking at the inflation that we see today, I think it's pretty clear if you look at not just the headline CPI numbers, but then you look at the core numbers, you look at trimmed mean and median, that what we're dealing with is primarily, if not exclusively, an energy shock. And in fact, we saw in those different ways that you can remove out buyers from the index, the inflation readings were continuing to fall until September, and now it's really just the last couple of months that we are seeing energy inflation, if you will, kind of spill out of the gas tank and hit everything else in the broader economy. 

So how does the Fed navigate something like an energy shock that we have today where the problem is not actually a monetary phenomenon, but instead the problem is really a supply shock? And if that's the case, how does that, if at all, change the way you and the Fed more broadly look at how they can use monetary tools to address what looks like a non-monetary problem? 

BOWMAN: EJ, that's a great question. And I address that in my remarks as well because generally with an energy shock, you try to look through that for as long as you can. But because we've been experiencing it for as long as we have, it is, I think over the last few inflation reports, we've seen that the inflation pressures have been broadening. And so we've reached the point where I don't think that you can as obviously look through them, especially as we have a strong labor market and we have a dual mandate, full employment and stable prices. So I think especially with today's CPI print, it just indicates to me that the time has come, for me anyway, to shift the focus to inflation and trying to lower inflation.
